The Johnny darter (Etheostoma nigrum) attains a maximum total length of 7.2 centimeters [Li = 7.2 centimeters], a modest size typical of the sand darter subgroup within the speciose genus Etheostoma. This ultimate body length is achieved gradually over the species' lifespan, with growth rates strongly modulated by seasonal temperature regimes in its preferred small-stream habitats. Reproductive development proceeds more slowly than in many darter congeners; individuals do not reach the standard length associated with puberty until approximately 3.3 centimeters [Lp = approximately 3.3 centimeters]. This size threshold signals the onset of gonadal maturation, after which individuals become capable of contributing to the population during the spring spawning season.

At the commencement of exogenous feeding, newly emerged larvae weigh approximately 0.0012 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0012 grams], a value derived from the egg diameter of roughly 1.3 millimeters, corresponding to a spherical volume estimate for the yolk-dependent embryo. This modest wet weight at birth reflects the limited provisioning typical of small-bodied benthic freshwater fishes, whose eggs are adhesive and deposited beneath stones in gravel-bottomed riffles. The yolk-sac larva relies entirely on endogenous reserves during the first few days post-hatching, with the mouth-closed prolarva gradually absorbing its yolk before the critical transition to active feeding on microcrustaceans.

Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at 13 °C [T = 13 °C], the maximum reproductive rate has been characterized through a fecundity of approximately 12 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 12 eggs per spawning event] and a spawning frequency of approximately 104 spawning events per year [F_R_i = approximately 104 spawning events per year], yielding a daily rate of approximately 3.4 offspring per day. This combination of modest clutch size and high spawning frequency positions Etheostoma nigrum as an iteroparous batch spawner, releasing multiple clutches of eggs over the extended spring period. The thermal regime strongly governs the timing and intensity of vitellogenesis and gamete release in this species.

The ultimate wet weight attained by adult Johnny darters is approximately 2.5 grams [Wwi = approximately 2.5 grams], a body mass that is consistent with the species' placement among the smaller members of the Etheostoma radiation. This asymptotic mass is reached after several growing seasons and is associated with the completion of somatic development prior to the onset of reproductive senescence. Field surveys indicate that females tend to achieve slightly greater body masses than males, likely reflecting the energetic demands of egg production and the volumetric constraints of gravid individuals carrying yolked oocytes.

Longevity records maintained at a stable temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C] indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 4 years [am = approximately 4 years] for Etheostoma nigrum under controlled conditions. This lifespan is relatively extended compared to some other small-bodied darter species, potentially reflecting the species' preference for cool, well-oxygenated headwater streams where metabolic demands are lower. Senescence in this species is gradual, with reproductively active adults observed in their third and fourth years before age-related declines in body condition and spawning success become apparent.
